analysis.one_liner: Speeds up mining permits on federal land and limits lawsuits against them.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap environmental reviews of mining projects at 18–24 months, limit lawsuits over mining permits, and expand miners' rights on public land died in House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal permitting rules so that mining projects on public land get an environmental review capped at 18 months (or 24 months for the most detailed reviews), with the clock adjustable at the mining company's request. It would have barred lawsuits against a mining permit filed more than a year after it was finalized, let exploration that disturbs up to 5 acres go forward with just a notice instead of a permit, and given mining claim holders a guaranteed right to use public land while treating their low annual claim fees as satisfying the government's fair-market-value requirement. It also would have extended rules written for "critical" minerals — the ones flagged for supply-chain reasons — to every kind of mineral.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies are the clear beneficiary. The bill targets the two things the industry identifies as its biggest costs on federal land: how long permitting takes (18-month and 24-month deadlines, extendable by agreement with the company) and how easily permits can be challenged in court (a one-year deadline for lawsuits). It would let companies start exploration disturbing up to 5 acres with only a notice to the government, guarantee claim holders the right to occupy public land before and after proving a deposit, and apply the supply-chain rules written for critical minerals to copper, nickel, gold, and every other mineral. The changes could apply even to applications already pending when the bill passed.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the environmental review clock for mining projects at 18 months for an environmental assessment and 24 months for an environmental impact statement, with extensions available through agreements with the project applicant, and lets applicants invoke these deadlines even for applications filed before the law took effect.

Bars any federal lawsuit challenging a mining permit, license, or approval unless it is filed within one year of the permit becoming final, sharply narrowing the window communities and conservation groups have to contest a project in court.

Expands the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act's critical-minerals permitting provisions to cover all minerals, requires federal agencies to defer to state agencies' baseline environmental data for mining projects, and directs agencies to set up coordinating agreements with a designated 'lead agency'.

Allows mineral exploration that disturbs up to 5 acres of federal land to proceed after the company simply files a notice describing the work and reclamation, rather than going through a full permitting process.

Gives mining claim holders a 'security of tenure' right to use and occupy public land before and after discovering a valuable deposit, and deems their claim maintenance and location fees sufficient to satisfy the fair-market-value requirements of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act — meaning the government could not charge them market rates for the use of public land.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on people who live near or use federal lands where mining could occur. They would face shorter and potentially shallower environmental reviews, only one year to sue over a finalized permit, exploration work on up to 5-acre patches that never goes through a permit process at all, and mining-related use of public land that the bill treats as fully paid for by low annual claim fees. Under the 1872 Mining Law, hardrock miners already pay no royalty on the minerals they take from federal land; this bill would add to what the public gives up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near mines and public-land users

drawbacks.text: The one-year limit on lawsuits means a resident or conservation group that learns of a flawed permit late, or takes time to build a case, could lose any ability to challenge it in court.

Fixed deadlines for environmental reviews, adjustable by unanimous agreement among the agencies and with extensions at the applicant's option, create pressure to complete reviews on schedule rather than thoroughly — and the bill directs agencies to rely on state baseline data rather than their own analysis.

The security-of-tenure provision lets claim holders use public land for mining and related activities while deeming modest annual claim fees to satisfy fair-market-value requirements, so taxpayers receive less than market value for the use of their land, on top of an 1872-era system in which hardrock miners pay no royalty on extracted minerals.

By stripping the word 'critical' from the supply-chain provisions, the bill extends fast-track treatment to all minerals, not just those deemed strategically important, so the national-security rationale does not match the scope of the benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument behind the bill: permitting for domestic minerals can take years, and faster review of projects needed for batteries, defense, and other supply chains has genuine value. But this bill does not confine itself to critical minerals — it applies to all mining on federal land — and its most consequential provisions cut in the other direction: a one-year lawsuit window, deadline pressure on environmental reviews, permit-free exploration on up to 5 acres, and a declaration that low claim fees satisfy the government's fair-market-value requirement. The gains to industry in speed and litigation protection are large and permanent; the public costs are diffuse, environmental, and long-lived. A narrower bill focused on genuinely critical minerals, without the judicial-review and tenure provisions, would have been far easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees, then to a Natural Resources subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stauber of Minnesota introduced the bill on September 20, 2022, joined by Rep. Bruce Westerman of Arkansas as its sole cosponsor, near the end of the 117th Congress.

It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and the Agriculture Committee, and on October 28, 2022, the Natural Resources Committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry — the last action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, as do all bills that do not pass in a two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who live near or use federal lands open to mining are better off, since the shortened reviews, one-year lawsuit window, and expanded claim-holder rights never took effect. The two Republican sponsors and the mining companies that would have benefited gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near mining projects and land users

for.name: Rep. Pete Stauber
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would speed permitting for mining on federal land, including the copper-nickel mining region of his northeastern Minnesota district.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Westerman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced.

for.name: Mining industry groups
for.what_they_did: Backed federal permitting reform for mining projects, pressing for shorter environmental review timelines and limits on litigation.

against.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill; after the October 28 subcommittee referral it received no further action.

against.name: Rep. David Scott
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no bill that does not clear committee can be scheduled for a vote, and none was.

against.name: Conservation and tribal community groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed bills limiting environmental review and judicial review of mining on federal land, as cutting off communities' ability to contest projects.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its two sponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic chairs of both committees it was referred to took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions — 18–24 month review deadlines, a one-year lawsuit window, notice-only exploration on up to 5 acres, and claim fees deemed to satisfy fair-market-value requirements — directly cut the industry's largest costs on federal land while leaving environmental and community interests with less process. Its supply-chain framing does not match its all-minerals scope.

industries.industry: Mining equipment, engineering, and mine-services firms
industries.note: Faster, harder-to-challenge permits mean more exploration and mine development moving ahead, which drives demand for the contractors and equipment suppliers that serve mining projects.

industries.industry: Public lands and outdoor recreation (users of federal land)
industries.note: This is a diffuse public interest rather than an industry, but it is the counterparty here: less environmental review, permit-free exploration patches, and mining use of public land at below market value would come at the expense of people who hunt, fish, and recreate on and near these lands.
